lead: Most machine parts carry a steady load with a vibration on top: a bolt tightened and then pulled by gas pressure, a spring preloaded and then cycled. The stress moves between a maximum and a minimum that are not equal and opposite. Splitting the cycle into a mean and an alternating stress turns it into one point on a diagram, and failure lines drawn from the endurance limit and the static strengths give the factor of safety.
prereq: You need: Se and the S–N line from fatigue and the S–N curve, equivalent stresses from theories of failure, and Kf from stress concentration.

sections.h3: From a stress cycle to one point

blocks.text: Let σ<sub>max</sub> and σ<sub>min</sub> be the largest and smallest stresses in the cycle, in MPa, with tension positive. Then:

σ<sub>m</sub> is the mean stress, σ<sub>a</sub> the alternating stress (half the range), both in MPa, and R the stress ratio. Put σ<sub>min</sub> in with its sign: for σ<sub>max</sub> = 150 MPa and σ<sub>min</sub> = −50 MPa, σ<sub>m</sub> = (150 + (−50))/2 = 50 MPa and σ<sub>a</sub> = (150 − (−50))/2 = 100 MPa.

Three cycles have names. Fully reversed: σ<sub>m</sub> = 0, R = −1 (a rotating shaft in bending). Repeated: σ<sub>min</sub> = 0, R = 0, σ<sub>m</sub> = σ<sub>a</sub> (a gear tooth that loads and unloads). Fluctuating: any other pair (a preloaded bolt).
Plot σ<sub>m</sub> along the horizontal axis and σ<sub>a</sub> up the vertical one (the Haigh diagram). The part is safe while its point stays inside the failure line.
Each fatigue line starts at S<sub>e</sub> on the σ<sub>a</sub> axis and ends at a static strength on the σ<sub>m</sub> axis; none is drawn past that intercept.

Soderberg is the lowest line because S<sub>yt</sub> < S<sub>ut</sub>, so it is the safest and also guards against yield. Goodman is the usual design line. Gerber bows outward and passes closest to test points for ductile steels, so it must be paired with the Langer line, which stops the peak stress σ<sub>a</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub> from reaching yield in the first cycle. A compressive mean stress does not shorten fatigue life; for σ<sub>m</sub> < 0 the usual rule is simply σ<sub>a</sub> ≤ S<sub>e</sub>/n.

sections.h3: Factor of safety, notches and finite life

blocks.text: Scale the working point by n until it reaches the chosen line:
Goodman: 1/n = σa/Se + σm/Sut Soderberg: 1/n = σa/Se + σm/Syt Gerber: (σm/Sut)² n² + (σa/Se) n − 1 = 0
n is the factor of safety; for Gerber take the positive root. Then check Langer: n<sub>y</sub> = S<sub>yt</sub>/(σ<sub>a</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>), and the smaller n governs.

Notches: multiply σ<sub>a</sub> by K<sub>f</sub> (many textbooks apply K<sub>f</sub> to the alternating part only for ductile materials, others to σ<sub>m</sub> as well; follow your prescribed book). Combined bending and torsion: build von Mises equivalents for each part, σ<sub>a,eq</sub> = √(σ<sub>a</sub>² + 3τ<sub>a</sub>²) and σ<sub>m,eq</sub> = √(σ<sub>m</sub>² + 3τ<sub>m</sub>²), and use them on the diagram.

Finite life: a part that need last only N cycles uses S<sub>f</sub> at N (from the S–N line) in place of S<sub>e</sub> in the same equations. Shaft codes such as ASME use an elliptic line in place of Goodman.

figure.caption: All three lines start at Se = 230 MPa. Soderberg meets Syt = 400 MPa, Goodman meets Sut = 600 MPa, and Gerber curves above Goodman.

spec.aria: Three failure lines starting at 230 MPa; Soderberg falls fastest to 400 MPa, Goodman reaches 600 MPa, and Gerber bows outward above Goodman.

examples.question: A shaft section sees σ<sub>max</sub> = 120 MPa and σ<sub>min</sub> = 40 MPa. The steel has S<sub>ut</sub> = 600 MPa, S<sub>yt</sub> = 400 MPa and S<sub>e</sub> = 230 MPa (already corrected). Find σ<sub>m</sub>, σ<sub>a</sub> and the factor of safety by Goodman, Soderberg and Gerber, and check first-cycle yield.
steps: Goodman: 1/n = 40/230 + 80/600 = 0.1739 + 0.1333 = 0.3072, so n = 3.25. The scaled point (260, 130) lies on the line.
Gerber's 4.06 is above 3.33, so with Gerber the part would yield first: the Gerber design value is n = 3.33. Goodman's 3.25 is below 3.33, so Goodman governs on its own.
examples.answer: σ<sub>m</sub> = 80 MPa, σ<sub>a</sub> = 40 MPa; n = 3.25 (Goodman), 2.67 (Soderberg), 3.33 (Gerber, limited by yield). Soderberg is the most conservative.

examples.question: A solid round bar is used as a beam that does not rotate. At its critical section the bending moment varies from 100 N·m to 400 N·m. The steel has S<sub>yt</sub> = 400 MPa and S<sub>e</sub> = 230 MPa (corrected), K<sub>f</sub> = 1.5 at the section, and n = 2. Find the diameter by the Soderberg line.
steps: Mean and alternating moments: M<sub>m</sub> = (400 + 100)/2 = 250 N·m = 250 000 N·mm; M<sub>a</sub> = (400 − 100)/2 = 150 N·m = 150 000 N·mm.
Stresses: σ<sub>m</sub> = 32M<sub>m</sub>/(πd³) and σ<sub>a</sub> = 32M<sub>a</sub>/(πd³), with K<sub>f</sub> on σ<sub>a</sub>.
examples.answer: d = 31.97 mm, rounded to 32 mm, which gives n = 2.01 by Soderberg.

traps: Swapping the axes. σ<sub>m</sub> goes along the horizontal axis and σ<sub>a</sub> up the vertical one; swapped, every intercept reads wrongly.
Pairing the wrong strength: Goodman with S<sub>yt</sub> or Soderberg with S<sub>ut</sub>. Goodman ends at S<sub>ut</sub>, Soderberg at S<sub>yt</sub>.
Scaling only one stress. The factor of safety multiplies both σ<sub>a</sub> and σ<sub>m</sub>; scaling σ<sub>a</sub> alone overstates n.
Quoting the Gerber n without the Langer check. In the first example Gerber gives 4.06 but the part yields at 3.33.
Using a Goodman-type line for a compressive mean stress. For σ<sub>m</sub> < 0 use σ<sub>a</sub> ≤ S<sub>e</sub>/n; the line would wrongly credit the compression.

quiz.q: Write σ<sub>m</sub>, σ<sub>a</sub> and R in terms of σ<sub>max</sub> and σ<sub>min</sub>.
quiz.a: σ<sub>m</sub> = (σ<sub>max</sub> + σ<sub>min</sub>)/2, σ<sub>a</sub> = (σ<sub>max</sub> − σ<sub>min</sub>)/2, R = σ<sub>min</sub>/σ<sub>max</sub>.

quiz.q: Why is the Soderberg line below the Goodman line for a ductile steel?
quiz.a: Both start at S<sub>e</sub>, but Soderberg ends at S<sub>yt</sub> and Goodman at S<sub>ut</sub>. Since S<sub>yt</sub> < S<sub>ut</sub>, the Soderberg line is lower everywhere and gives the smaller n.

quiz.q: A part has σ<sub>m</sub> = 100 MPa, σ<sub>a</sub> = 50 MPa, S<sub>e</sub> = 200 MPa, S<sub>ut</sub> = 500 MPa and S<sub>yt</sub> = 350 MPa. Find n by Goodman and Soderberg.
For σ<sub>m</sub> = 120 MPa, σ<sub>a</sub> = 60 MPa, S<sub>e</sub> = 240 MPa and S<sub>ut</sub> = 600 MPa, find n by Gerber.
Which line on the σ<sub>a</sub>–σ<sub>m</sub> diagram is a yield check rather than a fatigue line?
quiz.a: The Langer line, σ<sub>a</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub> = S<sub>yt</sub>. It stops the peak stress from reaching yield.

quiz.q: A cycle has σ<sub>max</sub> = 200 MPa and σ<sub>min</sub> = −100 MPa. Find σ<sub>m</sub>, σ<sub>a</sub> and R.
Why must a Gerber design always be checked with the Langer line, while a Soderberg design need not be?
quiz.a: The Gerber parabola bows outside the Langer line near the σ<sub>m</sub> axis, so a point inside Gerber can still reach yield. The Soderberg line ends at S<sub>yt</sub> and lies inside the Langer line everywhere, so it already guards against yield.

beyond: Not for the exam. Shaft design programs check Goodman, Gerber and the ASME elliptic line together and report the one that governs. Spring and bolt standards build these diagrams into their allowable stresses. Research extends them to variable-amplitude loads, multiaxial stress and the statistical scatter of Se. Search for 'Haigh diagram', 'modified Goodman diagram' and 'ASME elliptic criterion'.
